items.prompt: What stays the same during a refactor?
choices: The observable behavior of the code
The number of lines in the file
The names of every function
items.explanation: Only the outputs stay fixed; structure, line count and names are free to change.

items.prompt: Which change is a refactor?
choices: Switching the discount from 10% to 12%
Splitting a function, same output
Adding a new gift-wrap option for orders
items.explanation: Only the split leaves every output unchanged.

items.prompt: Can you stop halfway through a refactor?
choices: No, half-finished code never runs
Only after the final commit is made
Yes, every step leaves working code
items.explanation: Each step preserves behavior, so any stopping point is a working state.

items.prompt: Which describes a rewrite?
choices: Behavior may change, at least for a while
Behavior is proven identical at each step
Only variable names are changed
items.explanation: A rewrite makes no promise that behavior stays the same.

items.prompt: How big is one refactoring step?
choices: A whole module at a time
Tiny and individually checkable
As large as the day allows
items.explanation: Small steps keep each check cheap and each failure easy to locate.

items.prompt: A change alters what a function returns for some input. Is it a refactor?
choices: Yes, because the code looks much cleaner afterward
Yes, if the tests are updated to match
No, behavior changed so it is something else
items.explanation: Looking tidier does not make it a refactor; unchanged behavior does.

items.prompt: What does a refactor aim to improve?
choices: How easy the code is to read and change
How many features the program has
How quickly the program starts up in production
items.explanation: Refactoring targets structure and changeability, not features.

items.prompt: Which is true of rewrites compared with refactors?
choices: They never need any tests at all
They need fresh tests
They are always the safer of the two
items.explanation: A rewrite changes behavior, so old tests may no longer apply.

items.prompt: Dana splits `calculateOrderTotal` into five smaller functions and, in the same pass, rounds tax to the nearest cent instead of leaving it unrounded. Which statement is accurate?
choices: The split is a refactor, but the rounding changes behavior, so it is mixed
The whole pass is a refactor, since splitting is the main goal of the change
The whole pass is a rewrite, since any edit to tax logic makes it one
Neither part is a refactor, since five functions are replacing one function
items.explanation: Rounding can change a returned total, so only the split alone qualifies as a refactor.
items.reference:
Same behavior, new structure
refactor: outputs identical before and after
rewrite: outputs may change, even briefly
refactor: tiny steps, each one checkable
rewrite: big bang, halfway is often broken
Why: refactoring is defined by one constraint: behavior unchanged from the outside.
items.learnMore:
Refactoring is not rewriting

A refactor changes how code is organized and promises the same inputs give the same outputs. Because of that promise, you can stop after any step and still have working code. A rewrite makes no such promise.

Common mistake

Calling any tidy-up a refactor even when it also changed what the code returns.
items.reflection: Think of tidying a shared kitchen without moving where anything is used. What would count as the 'behavior' that must not change?

items.prompt: Two teams disagree. One says 'we refactored the checkout module', the other says 'we rewrote it'. Which fact would settle who is right?
choices: Whether the diff touched more than half the lines in the module
Whether every input still produces the same output as before
Whether the new code was written by the original author
Whether the module now has fewer files than it had before
items.explanation: The defining test is unchanged observable behavior, not diff size, authorship or file count.

choices: It was a rewrite that happened to work, which is the usual outcome
It was abandoned and nothing in production depends on it
Each step likely preserved behavior, as a refactor should
The tests were deleted, so nothing could notice a difference
items.explanation: Refactor steps leave working code, so a half-done refactor is still safe to ship.

items.prompt: A tidy-up PR renames variables, extracts a helper and, to simplify, drops a check that 'can never fire'. Why is calling it a refactor risky?
choices: Renaming variables is never allowed inside a refactoring step
Extracting a helper always changes the results a function returns
Refactors may not touch any file that already has tests
The dropped check may change behavior in a case nobody tested
items.explanation: Removing logic may alter outputs for untested inputs, which a refactor must not do.

items.prompt: A tangled function has no tests. What is the first safe move?
choices: Start extracting small helper functions
Write tests that record what it does today
Rewrite it cleanly from the ground up this week
items.explanation: Without tests there is nothing to check a refactor against.

items.prompt: What is a characterization test?
choices: A test that checks the ideal intended behavior
A test that measures how fast the code runs
A test that records current behavior as it is
items.explanation: It pins down what the code does today, quirks included.

items.prompt: Without tests, what does 'I did not change behavior' amount to?
choices: An opinion with nothing to back it up
A proven fact about the new code
A guarantee from the compiler
items.explanation: Only an automated check can turn the claim into evidence.

items.prompt: A function has an odd quirk. What should its characterization test do?
choices: Skip the quirk until it is understood
Record the quirk exactly as it behaves
Assert the behavior the author likely wanted
items.explanation: The test documents what happens today; fixing is a separate decision.

items.prompt: When are characterization tests written?
choices: After the refactor is fully finished
Only once a bug has been reported
Before any structural change
items.explanation: They are the net that must exist before the first step.

items.prompt: What does 'no tests' mean for a refactor?
choices: The safe move is not available yet
Just be extra careful and carry on
The code must be thrown away instead
items.explanation: Care is not a substitute for a check; the net has to come first.

items.prompt: Which result do characterization tests give on the untouched code?
choices: A mix of passes and failures
All of them pass
None of them can be run yet
items.explanation: They describe current behavior, so the original code passes them.

items.prompt: Why record a quirk instead of fixing it in the test?
choices: Quirks are never worth fixing in code
Tests are not allowed to describe known bugs at all
A fixed test would fail a correct refactor
items.explanation: If the test assumes new behavior, preserving the old behavior looks like a failure.

items.prompt: Dana has no time to write tests first and says she will 'just be very careful'. What is wrong with that plan?
choices: Careful programmers should never refactor code that lacks tests
Care cannot show that behavior is unchanged, only a check can
Tests would only slow her down without catching anything useful
Being careful works, but only if a second person reviews each line
items.explanation: Without a check the 'unchanged' claim stays unverified however careful she is.
items.reference:
Tests before tidying
no tests: 'behavior unchanged' is only an opinion
write tests that record what runs today
quirks included, not just intended behavior
only then change structure
Why: the claim a refactor makes needs something that can check it.
items.learnMore:
Characterization tests

A characterization test records what the code does now, not what it should do. It gives every later step something honest to be compared against, even when the current behavior looks odd.

Common mistake

Writing tests for what the code ought to do, so a correct refactor appears to fail.
items.reflection: Think of copying a recipe before editing it. Where else would you save a record of how things work today before changing them?

items.prompt: A characterization test is written to assert what the author believes the discount ought to be. The refactor preserves today's real output and the test fails. Where is the fault?
choices: In the refactor, which should have matched the test's expected value
In the original code, which must be fixed before anything else
In the test, which described intent instead of current behavior
In the test runner, which compares numbers in an unreliable way
items.explanation: Characterization tests must record what happens now; otherwise they blame correct work.

choices: A faster refactor that carries slightly more risk than usual
A refactor that is fine as long as commits are small
A refactor that only matters for code in public libraries
An unverified rewrite that only carries a refactor's name
items.explanation: With nothing to check behavior against, the work is a rewrite in all but name.

choices: To record current behavior, so a later fix is a visible change
To prove the function is correct for every input it will ever see
To make the suite fail until somebody repairs the function
To avoid writing any test for the inputs that behave correctly
items.explanation: Recording the wrong answer keeps a later correction a separate, intentional step.

items.prompt: What is a code smell?
choices: A syntax error the compiler refuses to accept
A bug that has already caused a failure
A hint that a design problem may exist
items.explanation: It is a hint to look closer, not proof of a defect.

items.prompt: The same check is written in three places. Which smell is that?
choices: Duplicated logic
Unnamed constants
Nested conditionals
items.explanation: Repeating the same logic in several places is duplication.

items.prompt: A bare `0.07` appears in the middle of a calculation. Which smell is it?
choices: Duplicated logic
A magic number
A long function
items.explanation: An unnamed value forces the reader to guess its meaning.

items.prompt: Four `if` blocks sit inside one another. Which smell is that?
choices: A magic number
Dead code
Deep nesting
items.explanation: Each level multiplies the paths a reader must follow.

items.prompt: Does a smell always mean the code must be rewritten now?
choices: No, it is a prompt to look closer
Yes, smells are always defects
Yes, but only in large functions
items.explanation: A smell is a prompt, not a rewrite order.

items.prompt: What goes wrong when one copy of duplicated logic gets a bug fix?
choices: All copies are fixed automatically by the tools
The other copies keep the old behavior
The function stops compiling entirely
items.explanation: Copies are independent, so they drift apart.

items.prompt: Why is a 68-line function a smell?
choices: Long functions always run more slowly
Most tools refuse to analyze such files
It is hard to hold in your head at once
items.explanation: The cost is human understanding, not machine speed.

items.prompt: Which is the best next step after spotting a smell?
choices: Decide whether it is worth acting on
Rewrite the whole file straight away
Ignore it because smells are harmless
items.explanation: Looking closer comes first; acting depends on its cost.

items.prompt: Boxtree's function checks 'real member' in three places. Two write `isMember && !membershipSuspended` and one writes only `isMember`. What is the main risk of this duplication?
choices: The function runs three times slower than a single check would
The compiler rejects three identical conditions in one function
The copies can silently disagree about who counts as a member
The extra checks use more memory every time the code is run
items.explanation: Separate copies drift: here one already differs from the other two.
items.reference:
Smells are prompts, not verdicts
duplicated logic: fix one copy, the other keeps the bug
long function: too much to hold in your head
deep nesting: each branch multiplies the paths
magic numbers: the reader has to guess
Why: a smell is a surface signal that a design problem probably lives underneath.
items.learnMore:
Reading code smells

A smell tells you where to look closer. It is not proof of a defect and not an order to rewrite. Whether to act depends on how often the code changes and what acting would cost.

Common mistake

Treating every smell as a bug that must be removed on sight.
items.reflection: Think of a strange noise from a car. How do you decide whether it needs attention now or can wait?

items.prompt: A 12-line function has a few `if` blocks, never changes, and is read by nobody. A teammate wants to refactor it for its smell. What is the sound response?
choices: Refactor it at once, since every smell is a defect to remove
Delete it, because code that nobody reads has no purpose
Rewrite it, because small functions are never worth keeping
A smell is a prompt; unchanging code may not earn the effort
items.explanation: Whether to act depends on how often the code changes and what acting costs.

choices: Deep nesting: every branch multiplies paths to follow
Magic numbers: the program crashes when the value is changed
Duplicated logic: the code takes twice as long to compile
Long function: the file can no longer be saved or committed
items.explanation: Nesting costs reasoning effort; the others invent costs that do not exist.

items.prompt: A reviewer says 'this function has three smells, so it is wrong'. Which correction is best?
choices: Smells and wrong behavior are the same thing, so she is right
Smells suggest where to look; wrong means incorrect behavior
Only duplication counts as a smell, so two of three do not

items.explanation: A function can smell and still compute the right answer.

items.prompt: What comes right after one small structural change?
choices: Run the full test suite
Start the next change immediately
Write the commit message for later
items.explanation: Each step is checked before the next one begins.

items.prompt: The suite is green after a step. What next?
choices: Wait and commit all steps together
Commit that step by itself
Delete the tests that just passed
items.explanation: A green step is committed alone so it can be reverted alone.

items.prompt: The suite goes red after a step. What does the loop say to do?
choices: Edit the failing test so that it passes again
Continue and repair it at the end
Revert that step and try a smaller one
items.explanation: The failure belongs to one step, so undo that step.

items.prompt: Why commit after every step?
choices: Each step can be reverted on its own
Git requires one commit per file
Commits make the tests run faster
items.explanation: Separate commits keep undo cheap and precise.

items.prompt: If step 3 of 6 fails, where is the problem?
choices: Somewhere among the first three steps taken
In step 3, since 1 and 2 were verified
Somewhere across all six steps
items.explanation: Earlier steps were already green, so only step 3 is new.

items.prompt: How many smells does one step address?
choices: All the smells in the function
As many as fit in an hour
One
items.explanation: One step, one smell, one verification.

items.prompt: What does a big single rewrite give you when a test fails?
choices: No clue about which change broke it
The exact line that caused it
A guarantee that it was a test bug
items.explanation: Many changes landed together, so the cause could be any of them.

items.prompt: What does reverting one small step cost?
choices: The whole day's progress
Minutes of work
A fresh set of tests to write
items.explanation: Only that step is lost, which is why small steps are cheap to undo.

items.prompt: Dana bundles six structural steps and tests once. Assume each step has an independent 5% chance of an undetected slip. What is the chance at least one slip got through?
choices: Exactly 30%, since the six chances of 5% simply add up
About 5%, since the same single test run covers every step
About 6%, since only the final step could carry a slip
About 26%, as it compounds: 1 minus 0.95 to the sixth
items.explanation: Independent risks compound: 1 - 0.95^6 is roughly 26.5%.
items.reference:
One step, test, commit or revert
1. smallest change for one smell
2. run the full suite
3. green: commit this step alone
3. red: revert this step, try a smaller one
Why: a failure then points at one step, and undoing it costs minutes.
items.learnMore:
Why small steps

If step 3 of six fails, steps 1 and 2 were already verified, so the search space is one step. In one big rewrite a failure could be anywhere in 68 changed lines.

Common mistake

Believing small steps are about how much work happens, rather than how much must be re-verified together.
items.reflection: Think of walking across ice by testing each foot placement. When would you choose a bigger stride, and what would it cost you?

items.prompt: Step 4 of a 6-step refactor turns the suite red. Which statement about the cause is justified?
choices: It is step 4, because steps 1 to 3 were verified green
It is unknowable, since the earlier steps might share the fault
It is step 6, because the last step is the riskiest one
It is the tests, because small steps almost never fail
items.explanation: Verified earlier steps shrink the search to the one new change.

items.prompt: A teammate says: 'more commits just means more overhead, I will commit once at the end of the cleanup'. What does that give up?
choices: The ability to run the tests more than a single time overall
The ability to tell which change broke things and undo it
The ability to keep working on any other task in parallel
The ability to write a commit message that is long enough
items.explanation: Frequent commits make failures local and reverts cheap.

items.prompt: The suite goes red after a step, and Dana thinks the test is wrong. What does the loop prescribe first?
choices: Edit the test so that it matches the new output you got
Disable the test until the end of the refactoring session
Revert the step, since it is the new, unverified change
Keep the change and add a second step to compensate
items.explanation: In a refactor the old tests are the authority; the step is what changed.

items.prompt: Which move fixes a magic number?
choices: Inline
Extract Variable
Guard clauses
items.explanation: Giving the value a name explains what it is.

items.prompt: Which move fixes a block repeated in three places?
choices: Extract Variable for each copy
Rename
Extract Function and reuse it
items.explanation: One shared function removes the repetition.

items.prompt: Which move fixes an `if` nested four levels deep?
choices: Guard clauses
Extract Variable
Rename
items.explanation: Early returns flatten the nesting.

items.prompt: An if/else chain branches on the same region value. Which move helps?
choices: Rename the variable
Replace it with a lookup table
Inline the function
items.explanation: A table keyed by region removes the repeated branching.

items.prompt: What does Rename fix?
choices: Duplicated logic
Deep nesting
A misleading identifier
items.explanation: It changes a name to say what the thing is.

items.prompt: What does Inline do?
choices: Folds a function back into its call site
Pulls a block of code out into its own function
Gives a number a name
items.explanation: It is the reverse of Extract.

items.prompt: When does Inline earn its place?
choices: Whenever a function has fewer than ten lines in it
When the indirection costs more than it helps
Never, since extraction is always better
items.explanation: Needless indirection is the smell Inline removes.

items.prompt: Does a refactoring move change what the code does?
choices: Yes, it changes the output slightly
Yes, but only for edge cases
No, it only changes structure
items.explanation: Every move preserves behavior by definition.

items.prompt: Dana's membership check appears three times with small differences. Which move targets the actual problem?
choices: Remove Duplication: one shared function used at every site
Extract Variable: give the repeated condition a name each time
Rename: pick a clearer name for each copy of the condition
Inline: fold all three checks into one longer expression
items.explanation: The smell is repeated logic, which one shared home fixes.
items.reference:
Each move answers one smell
magic numbers: Extract Variable
long function: Extract Function
duplicated logic: Extract and reuse
deep nesting: guard clauses or a lookup table
misleading name: Rename
Why: a move is the smallest change that fixes one smell, nothing more.
items.learnMore:
Matching moves to smells

The catalog is useful because it pairs a named, small change with a named problem. Pick the move from what is actually wrong: an unnamed value needs a name, a repeated rule needs one shared home.

Common mistake

Reaching for Extract Function for everything, including repeated logic where the problem is the repetition.
items.reflection: Think of organizing a toolbox. Which kinds of mess call for labelling, which for gathering duplicates, which for removing a layer?

items.prompt: A shipping block nests a price threshold inside each region branch. Which move reduces the nesting most directly?
choices: Extract Variable for the threshold value of 75 only
Guard clause plus a lookup table keyed by region
Rename the shipping variable so it reads better
Inline the shipping function into its only caller
items.explanation: A guard handles the threshold once; the table handles the region.

items.prompt: A helper `getValue(x)` only returns `x.value` and is called in one place. Which move fits?
choices: Extract Function, to make the helper even smaller
Remove Duplication, because the name appears twice
Inline, since the indirection adds nothing
Replace Conditional with a lookup table
items.explanation: A wrapper that earns nothing is exactly what Inline removes.

items.prompt: A commit both restructures code and adds a feature. What is the problem?

The feature will run more slowly
Neither change can be checked on its own
items.explanation: Two questions are mixed into one answer.

items.prompt: What does a refactor commit claim?

A new feature works
The code is now faster

items.prompt: What does a feature commit claim?

The new behavior is correct
The structure is cleaner now

items.prompt: Where should the line between refactor and feature be drawn?

Between different files only
At the commit boundary
items.explanation: Separate commits keep each check independent.

items.prompt: Can one pull request hold both a refactor and a feature?

No, never under any circumstance
Only if the feature is tiny
items.explanation: The PR can include both as long as commits are separate.

items.prompt: In a feature commit, what is expected of the tests?
choices: No test is allowed to change under any circumstance
New tests are added for the new behavior
All tests are deleted and rewritten
items.explanation: New behavior needs new checks.

items.prompt: In a refactor commit, what is expected of the tests?
choices: Tests are updated to match new output
New tests cover brand-new behavior
Existing tests pass unchanged
items.explanation: If a test must change, behavior changed.

items.prompt: Why is a test that must change a warning sign in a refactor?
choices: It suggests behavior changed
Tests should never be edited at all
It means the code is faster
items.explanation: A refactor leaves old tests green as they are.

items.prompt: A PR restructures `calculateOrderTotal` and adds a loyalty discount in one diff. A test fails. Why is the failure hard to interpret?

Tests cannot run on a diff that touches more than one function
The restructuring cannot fail, so the discount code must be at fault
items.explanation: Two changes with two different verification questions have blurred together.
items.reference:

refactor commit: did behavior stay the same?
check: existing tests, unchanged, still pass
feature commit: is the new behavior correct?
check: new tests, written for it, pass

items.prompt: What does a suspended member pay for gift wrap today?
choices: 1.50, the member rate
2.99, the standard rate
Nothing at all
items.explanation: The branch checks only isMember, so suspended members get 1.50.

items.explanation: It skips the suspension flag the other branches use.

items.prompt: Should the Step 3 extraction change the gift-wrap branch?

items.explanation: Changing it would alter a customer's total.

choices: A suspended member's gift fee
The shipping rate for all regions
The tax rate for the EU
items.explanation: The fee would move from 1.50 to 2.99.

items.prompt: How would the suite notice that change?
choices: Nothing in the suite would notice it at all
The suspended-member case would go red
The EU case would go red
items.explanation: That case records today's real 59.99 total.

items.prompt: Is the gift-wrap inconsistency worth fixing?
choices: No, quirks must never be fixed
Yes, silently, inside the refactor
Possibly, as a separate decision
items.explanation: Whether it is wrong is a product call, made later.

items.prompt: A suspended member orders a 50 item to the US with gift wrap. What total is recorded?
items.explanation: 50 + 4.99 shipping + 3.50 tax + 1.50 gift fee = 59.99.

items.prompt: Why list the odd case among the six tests?
choices: To prove suspended members should pay less
To record today's behavior, not approve it
To make the suite fail on purpose
items.explanation: Documenting a quirk keeps later steps honest.

items.prompt: During Step 3 Dana notices gift wrap ignores the suspension flag. She is tempted to switch it to `isActiveMember` in the same commit. What should she do?
choices: Switch it, since matching the other two is the point of the extraction
Switch it and quietly update the failing test to the new total
Leave it, then raise it as a separate, deliberate behavior change
Delete the gift-wrap test because it describes a bug
items.explanation: The commit's claim is 'nothing changed'; this change breaks that claim.
items.reference:
Preserve first, decide later
gift fee branch checks only isMember
suspended member pays 1.50 today
refactor leaves that exactly as it is
fixing it = its own commit, test updated on purpose
Why: a refactor may act on inconsistency, but may not change a real customer's total.
items.learnMore:
Quirks during a refactor

Noticing that three checks disagree is information. Deciding which one is right is a product decision. The refactor preserves what customers are charged and hands the decision to a separate, visible commit.

Common mistake

Fixing the odd branch while extracting the shared one, because it is right there.

items.prompt: Implement `sumRates(...rates)`: return the sum of all the numbers passed in (no cap). An empty call returns 0.
items.explanation: reduce with a starting value of 0 also covers the empty case.

items.explanation: Sum first, then compare strictly with greater-than, so exactly 20 is not over.

items.prompt: Implement `combineDiscountPercents(...percents)`: the sum of all percentages, capped at 20. With no arguments it returns 0.
items.explanation: Sum with an initial 0, then take the smaller of the total and the cap. The empty case falls out of the initial value.

Rates add up, then a cap applies
member 10% + bulk 5% + loyalty 10% = 25%
cap at 20% so the discount is 60 on a 300 order
sum first, then take the smaller of total and cap
new rule = new behavior = its own commit
Why: the cap is new logic the feature needs, so it belongs in the commit that changes behavior.
items.learnMore:
Capping combined rates

Because discount is a sum of rates after Step 5a, the loyalty tier is one more term and the cap is one final minimum. The order matters: cap the total, not each rate.

Common mistake

Capping each rate separately, which lets the combined total pass the limit.

Knowing when to stop
